item.title: OpenSSH Password Authentication Bypass on Alpine Linux (*sshole) – CVE-2026-123158
item.dc:creator: Moshe Siman Tov Bustan
item.description:

The post OpenSSH Password Authentication Bypass on Alpine Linux (*sshole) – CVE-2026-123158 appeared first on OX Security.
item.content:encoded:
A decade-old vulnerability in OpenSSH allows attackers to bypass password authentication on vulnerable Alpine Linux systems simply by entering an unusually long password. Tracked as CVE-2026-123158, the flaw can grant unauthorized access to accounts configured to reject password logins, potentially leading to root-level access on affected cloud systems. OpenSSH and Alpine Linux released fixes on November 5, 2026.

Overview

On November 5, 2026, OpenSSH released version 10.6p2 to address a password authentication bypass affecting Linux systems that use musl libc without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), including Alpine Linux’s default OpenSSH server configuration.

The vulnerability allows an attacker to authenticate to certain password-disabled accounts using an arbitrary password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long. No knowledge of the account’s actual credentials is required.

The underlying issue dates back to 2016 and results from the interaction of password-handling behavior in OpenSSH, musl libc, and Linux account configurations. Under specific conditions, a failed password-hashing operation produces the same value used to indicate that an account has no valid password. OpenSSH mistakenly interprets the matching values as successful authentication.

The impact extends beyond traditional Linux servers. Alpine Linux is widely used in cloud environments, containers, and lightweight infrastructure, while musl-based systems also appear in routers and embedded devices.

On affected Alpine cloud images, successful authentication to a default user with passwordless doas privileges can allow an attacker to escalate to root.

The vulnerability was reported to OpenSSH by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH and Alpine Linux have released patches, and administrators should update affected systems immediately.

Affected Versions

Alpine pushed the fix to every branch back to 3.16, including releases that are no longer supported:

Who Is Affected

You are affected if all of these are true:

  • Your SSH server runs on musl (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto).
  • It does not use PAM. Alpine’s openssh-server package doesn’t by default, or you set UsePAM no.
  • Password logins are on. They are by default.
  • There’s an account with no password set (shown as *): key-only users, LDAP users, root on Alpine.
  • And at least one other account on the box has a real password.

On Alpine’s official AWS and Azure images, that passwordless account is the default alpine user, and it can run doas (a lightweight sudo alternative) without a password. On vulnerable systems with this configuration, an attacker who gains access to the alpine account can effectively obtain root privileges.

Who Is Not Affected

The vulnerability does not affect:

  • Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, and other systems using glibc rather than musl for this authentication path.
  • SSH servers using PAM for password authentication.
  • Systems with PasswordAuthentication no.
  • Accounts whose password field contains ! rather than *.
  • Containers that do not run an OpenSSH server.
  • Systems without the required local password-hash configuration.
  • Dropbear and OpenBSD’s SSH implementation.

Technical Analysis: How CVE-2026-123158 Works

The vulnerability stems from three separate software decisions made over more than a decade. Individually, each had a reasonable purpose. Together, they created a way to bypass password authentication.

1. musl libc: A Password-Length Limit

Linux systems store password hashes in /etc/shadow. When a user attempts to authenticate, the SSH server checks the supplied password against the stored hash.

On musl libc, the crypt() password-hashing function refuses inputs longer than 256 bytes, a limit intended to prevent excessively long passwords from consuming unnecessary processing resources.

When hashing fails because the password exceeds that limit, musl returns the string *.

That value is significant because Linux also uses * in /etc/shadow to indicate that an account has no valid password hash and should not accept password authentication.

2. OpenSSH, 2016: A Change to Prevent Username Enumeration

In 2016, OpenSSH introduced password-checking behavior intended to reduce information leaks that could help attackers determine whether a username exists.

As part of that behavior, OpenSSH could perform a password-hashing operation using settings obtained from another account, even when the target account had no valid password hash.

On musl-based systems without PAM, this created an unexpected interaction with musl’s handling of excessively long passwords.

3. Alpine Linux, 2022: Password-Disabled Accounts

Beginning with Alpine Linux 3.16, the default root account used * in its password field, allowing SSH key authentication while preventing ordinary password logins.

Other accounts, including key-only users and the default user on certain Alpine cloud images, can also have this configuration.

This created the final condition necessary for the bypass.

How the Authentication Bypass Happens

When an attacker submits a password longer than 256 bytes to an eligible account whose stored password field is *, the following sequence occurs:

  1. The SSH server receives the authentication request.
  2. musl’s crypt() function rejects the oversized password and returns *.
  3. OpenSSH compares the returned value with the target account’s stored password field.
  4. Both values are *.
  5. The comparison succeeds, and the server accepts the login.

The attack requires no password guessing, stolen credentials, or repeated authentication attempts. When all vulnerable conditions are present, a single login attempt can succeed.

This is not a cryptographic weakness or a memory-corruption vulnerability. It is an authentication logic failure caused by the interaction between two components that interpret the same value differently.

How OpenSSH Fixed the Vulnerability

OpenSSH 10.6p2 prevents the authentication bypass by rejecting stored password hashes that are too short to represent a valid hash.

As a result, the * returned by a failed hashing operation can no longer be mistaken for a legitimate password match.

Recommended Actions

Immediate Actions:

  1. Update OpenSSH and restart it. On Alpine, run apk upgrade -U -a, then rc-service sshd restart. Updating the package alone doesn’t replace the SSH server that’s already running.
  2. Can’t update yet? Turn off password logins. Make sure your SSH key works first, then run echo “PasswordAuthentication no” > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf and restart sshd.
  3. Rebuild your images. Patching a running server isn’t enough if your Docker or cloud images still have the old package. Rebuild them from a fixed base and redeploy.
  4. Check if someone already got in. Search /var/log/messages for Accepted password for on an account that has no password (alpine, root, key-only users). If you find one, treat the machine as compromised.
  5. Block off public and unused ports, enforce VPN connections if possible to reduce the login bypass attack surface.
  • Be wary of PoCs and “checker” scripts. Do not clone or run unverified exploit or scanner scripts from public repos or social media; trust the OpenSSH release and your distribution’s official packages.

Conclusions

For ten years, this bug went unnoticed, which is both surprising and a little absurd when you think about it. This is exactly the kind of thing you’d expect to find in a regular QA session, where someone inevitably asks, “What happens if we try a really weird password?”

Looking at the research documented at sshhole.com, it took a brute-force approach to find it: building sshd in every combination of glibc, musl, PAM and no PAM, then throwing roughly 17,600 deliberately unusual login attempts at each build. Every build behaved the same except one: musl without PAM, which said yes when it should have said no.

The bug wasn’t hiding in some clever cryptography. It was sitting in the boring glue between OpenSSH and libc, the code few people bother to read. And all it took to expose it was a question as simple as: “What if the password is really long?”

We’re probably going to see a lot more of this. AI is making it possible to test software in ways that used to require the patience, curiosity and slightly obsessive mindset of hackers in the ’90s. Old software, weird edge cases, combinations nobody thought to test. There’s probably a lot more hiding in plain sight.

The post OpenSSH Password Authentication Bypass on Alpine Linux (*sshole) – CVE-2026-123158 appeared first on OX Security.

item.title: PolinRider Returns: Hijacked npm Packages Use Ethereum Blockchain to Conceal Malware Infrastructure
item.dc:creator: Moshe Siman Tov Bustan
item.description:
Overview OX Security researchers identified malicious releases of legitimate npm packages compromised in a campaign linked to the PolinRider malware family. The injected code uses the Ethereum blockchain as a dead drop for command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. When an affected package is imported, a hidden loader queries public Ethereum RPC endpoints to retrieve a C2 IP […]

The post PolinRider Returns: Hijacked npm Packages Use Ethereum Blockchain to Conceal Malware Infrastructure appeared first on OX Security.
item.content:encoded:
Overview

OX Security researchers identified malicious releases of legitimate npm packages compromised in a campaign linked to the PolinRider malware family.

The injected code uses the Ethereum blockchain as a dead drop for command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. When an affected package is imported, a hidden loader queries public Ethereum RPC endpoints to retrieve a C2 IP address encoded in a blockchain transaction. It then downloads an XOR-obfuscated JavaScript payload over HTTP and executes it.

This technique allows attackers to change the infrastructure used to deliver malicious code without modifying the compromised npm packages themselves. By updating the blockchain-based reference, attackers can redirect affected installations to new infrastructure while leaving the published package code unchanged.

The campaign uses two obfuscation techniques to conceal the loader: Base64-encoded JavaScript and a character-permutation bootstrap. Researchers also identified execution through an interactive Node.js process, allowing malicious code to run in memory and potentially complicating detection.

Recommended Actions

  1. Check for affected versions. Review installed dependencies and lockfiles for the compromised package versions listed below. Installation alone does not necessarily mean the malicious payload executed.
  2. Investigate potential wallet compromise. If an affected package was loaded and the malicious code executed, treat cryptocurrency wallets and associated credentials accessible from that environment as potentially compromised.
  3. Restrict dependency updates. Pin dependencies to verified clean versions and consider implementing a minimum package-age policy to reduce exposure to newly published malicious releases.

Impact

  • The affected packages collectively account for approximately 1,400 weekly downloads. This figure reflects package download activity, not confirmed infections or executions of the malicious payload.

Threat Analysis

We identified a multi-stage attack in which malicious code embedded in npm packages uses obfuscation, Ethereum-based command-and-control infrastructure, and in-memory execution to deliver additional payloads.

The following diagram illustrates the attack chain, from the initial malicious code in index.js to the retrieval and execution of a remote payload.

Inside the index.js file, researchers identified a hidden eval(atob(…)) function that decodes and executes a malicious Base64-encoded payload.

After decoding it, we can see the crypto stealer logic, with the threat actor’s ETH crypto address inside: 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3

It uses the “node -i” command to run everything inside the memory, indicating fileless execution which avoids detection.

The malware builds and resolves multiple IP addresses which are used as a C2 server.

We found the following IP addresses being used by the malware –  103[.]179[.]143[.]219, 166[.]88[.]134[.]75, 23[.]27[.]13[.]72, 95[.]135[.]181[.]151

After downloading the remote payload from the server, the malware executes it using the same node -i command described above.

Affected Packages

Conclusion

PolinRider’s return comes just a week after the reported Binance hack, underscoring the relentless targeting of cryptocurrency and software supply chains. Even major cryptocurrency thefts have not brought an end to these campaigns.

With approximately 1,400 combined weekly downloads across the affected packages, this campaign highlights the continued risks of npm account hijacking.

Attackers don’t need to create malicious packages from scratch when they can hijack legitimate ones. Despite years of efforts to secure npm accounts and packages, the registry remains a valuable target for threat actors.

IOCs

  • 103[.]179[.]143[.]219
  • 166[.]88[.]134[.]75
  • 23[.]27[.]13[.]72
  • 95[.]135[.]181[.]151

The post PolinRider Returns: Hijacked npm Packages Use Ethereum Blockchain to Conceal Malware Infrastructure appeared first on OX Security.

item.title: Compromised Claude Code extensions (versions 2.1.312 & 2.1.313) in Cursor try to install a backdoor
item.dc:creator: Nir Zadok
item.description:
Maliciously modified versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension run malicious code that attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor. Overview On October 29, 2026, maliciously modified versions of the `Anthropic.claude-code` extension, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS, were available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace between about 2:27 AM and […]

The post Compromised Claude Code extensions (versions 2.1.312 & 2.1.313) in Cursor try to install a backdoor appeared first on OX Security.
item.content:encoded:
Maliciously modified versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension run malicious code that attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor.

Overview

On October 29, 2026, maliciously modified versions of the `Anthropic.claude-code` extension, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS, were available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace between about 2:27 AM and 1:35 PM PT. The malicious versions were not developed by Anthropic.

The malicious code collects and reports host and user information, attempts to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to `authorized_keys`, enable the local SSH service and open a reverse SSH tunnel, and attempts to make the reverse SSH tunnel persistent.

The malicious version was removed from the marketplace and further distribution was blocked. The marketplace was shut down, its keys were rotated, and it was rebuilt and brought back online. The malicious server was taken offline with the hosting provider. An access audit confirmed no other extensions were tampered with. Uninstalling the extension may not be sufficient: the payload drops standalone persistence scripts that keep running.

What is the Claude Code extension?

Claude Code is Anthropic’s AI coding tool. Cursor, an AI code editor built on VS Code, distributes the Claude Code extension through its own VS Code extension marketplace. It was this marketplace—not Anthropic’s official distribution—that was compromised and used to distribute the malicious build.

Compromised Packages

Cursor reports no evidence that other versions of the extension, or the official distribution, are affected.

Stage 1 – Host reconnaissance

The malicious code collects information about the host and user, including the hostname, username, operating system, architecture, home directory path, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git email, and public IP address.

Cursor also identified lookups to ifconfig[.]me and api[.]ipify[.]org to determine the host’s public IP. Both are legitimate services, and connections to them alone should not be treated as an indicator of compromise.

Stage 2 – SSH backdoor key and reverse tunnel

The malicious code appends an attacker-controlled ssh-ed25519 public key, labeled svc-telemetry, to the user’s SSH authorized_keys file. It then attempts to enable the local SSH service and establish a reverse SSH tunnel to tunnel@134[.]209[.]82[.]225 over TCP port 22.

Command lines identified by Cursor include:

  • ssh -N -R ‘*:0:localhost:22’ and autossh -M 0
  • SSH options StrictHostKeyChecking=no, UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null, ServerAliveInterval=30, ServerAliveCountMax=3, ExitOnForwardFailure=yes, IdentitiesOnly=yes
  • systemsetup -setremotelogin on (macOS)
  • Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name OpenSSH.Server~~~~0.0.1.0 (Windows)

Enabling the local SSH service requires administrator privileges, which the extension typically would not have. According to Cursor, errors in the malicious code meant this step failed except in highly unusual circumstances where Cursor was launched with administrator privileges. As a result, the attacker could not log in through the tunnel on those hosts.

However, the failed SSH-service step does not mean the payload was harmless: the extension still adds the attacker’s SSH key, installs persistence, and sends host information to the attacker.

Stage 3 – Persistence

The payload installs persistence mechanisms designed to keep the reverse SSH tunnel running independently of the extension, with background scripts retrying the connection approximately every 60 seconds.

  • macOS — Creates a LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist (label com.apple.sysmond). Associated files include ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk, and $TMPDIR/.stk_<10 hex>.
  • Windows — Creates a scheduled task named SysMon that attempts to run as SYSTEM, with a fallback Startup script at %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\sysmon.cmd. Associated files include %USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd, %USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk, and %TEMP%\.stk_<10 hex>.

Stage 4 – Beacon

The malicious code reports host information and backdoor status via HTTP POST to hxxp://134[.]209[.]82[.]225:8099/beacon. It also attempts to send a beacon to 127[.]0[.]1:8099/beacon on the local host.

According to Cursor, the attacker-controlled server has since been taken offline. As a result, the external beacon and reverse SSH tunnel are no longer functional.

Am I affected?

The malicious extension adds an attacker-controlled SSH public key labeled svc-telemetry to the victim’s SSH authorized_keys file. If this key is present, the machine is impacted.

macOS:

grep -qs svc-telemetry ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && echo “svc-telemetry key found” || echo “No key found; machine not impacted”

Windows (PowerShell):

$files = “$HOME.ssh\authorized_keys”, “C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys” | Where-Object { Test-Path $_ }

if ($files -and (Select-String svc-telemetry $files)) { “svc-telemetry key found” } else { “No key found; machine not impacted” }

Recommendations

Per Cursor’s guidance, if you installed or updated to Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.313 from the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace between 2:27 AM and 1:35 PM PT on October 29, 2026:

  • Check for impact: Run the check above and search endpoint, network, and extension-installation telemetry for the indicators below.
  • Isolate affected hosts: Isolate any systems showing evidence of payload execution or backdoor installation.
  • Remediate: Remove the unauthorized SSH key, persistence mechanisms, and running tunnel processes, and assess whether the host should be rebuilt. Uninstalling the extension alone may not be sufficient.
  • Rotate credentials: From a trusted system, rotate credentials and sessions that were accessible from affected hosts. The limited environment-variable collection does not rule out subsequent credential access through the backdoor.

Indicators of Compromise

Package

Payload

Network

SSH

Files and persistence

Process / command line

  • `ssh -N -R ‘*:0:localhost:22’`, `autossh -M 0`
  • SSH options: `StrictHostKeyChecking=no`, `UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null`, `ServerAliveInterval=30`, `ServerAliveCountMax=3`, `ExitOnForwardFailure=yes`, `IdentitiesOnly=yes`
  • `schtasks /create /tn SysMon`
  • `systemsetup -setremotelogin on`
  • `Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name OpenSSH.Server~~~~0.0.1.0`

Takeaway

From the victim’s side, nothing suspicious had to be clicked and no vulnerability had to be exploited. Modified builds of two versions of a trusted AI coding extension, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, published under the real `Anthropic.claude-code` name, arrived through the editor’s own marketplace and were available for about 11 hours. As this case shows, an extension update can write to a developer’s SSH keys, register startup tasks and open network tunnels. A poisoned update to a trusted extension is code execution on the developer’s machine.

The cleanup does not end at the uninstall button. The payload was built to outlive the extension: an SSH key in `authorized_keys`, a LaunchAgent or scheduled task, and scripts that retry the tunnel roughly every 60 seconds. Even where the tunnel failed, the key and persistence stayed behind. Anyone who installed 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 should run the check above. If the key is found, isolate the host, confirm the key, persistence and tunnel processes are gone, and rotate every credential that host could reach.

The post Compromised Claude Code extensions (versions 2.1.312 & 2.1.313) in Cursor try to install a backdoor appeared first on OX Security.

item.title: Introducing Agent Activity: See What Your AI Agents Are Actually Doing
item.dc:creator: Sagiv Peer
item.description:
TL;DR For the past year, the first question security teams asked about AI was simple: do we have agents running, and where? That question now has an answer. The harder one is what comes next: what are those agents actually doing? Today we’re introducing Agent Activity, now in early access as part of OX.VibeSec and […]

The post Introducing Agent Activity: See What Your AI Agents Are Actually Doing appeared first on OX Security.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

  • See every step: Agent Activity traces each agent session’s prompts, MCP and tool calls, read/write access, and sensitive data touches.
  • Control what’s allowed: Custom guardrails by model, MCP server, and skill let you flag or block, starting from 100+ built-in policies.
  • Endpoint to production: It’s now in early access across OX.VibeSec and OX.Cloud, with a new LiteLLM connector.

For the past year, the first question security teams asked about AI was simple: do we have agents running, and where? That question now has an answer. The harder one is what comes next: what are those agents actually doing?

Today we’re introducing Agent Activity, now in early access as part of OX.VibeSec and OX.Cloud. It gives security teams step-by-step visibility into how their AI agents behave at runtime, and the controls to decide what those agents are allowed to do.

Agents move faster than static scans

AI agents don’t sit still long enough to be secured by a scan. They call MCP servers, invoke tools, read and write to business systems, and touch sensitive data, often in seconds and often without a human in the loop.

Discovery tells you an agent exists. Code scanning tells you how it was built. Runtime anomaly detection tells you something unusual happened. None of them tells you, step by step, what an agent did with the access it was given. That’s the gap Agent Activity closes.

Every step, not just the outcome

Agent Activity opens up what has been a black box. For each agent session, security teams can trace the full chain of actions from start to finish:

  • Prompts and responses: what the agent was asked, the instructions it worked from, and what came back.
  • MCP interactions and tool usage: which MCP servers and tools the agent called, and in what order.
  • Access permissions: whether the agent was reading or writing, so you can tell the difference between an agent that views a ticket and one that modifies it, or one that reads Slack and one that posts to it.
  • Sensitive data awareness: when an agent interacts with PII, secrets, tokens, or financial data, and when that data is at risk of leaving where it belongs.

In many cases, that visibility is enough to answer the question any security engineer or leader is being asked. When it isn’t, for example when an agent that leaked an API key also touched financial records, you need to act on it.

From visibility to control

No two organizations secure AI the same way. Some agents are meant to run freely; others should never come near production data. Agent Activity lets each team define what “allowed” means for its own environment.

  • Customizable runtime guardrails: build policies around the AI models in use, the MCP servers agents can reach, and the skills they can combine. For example, you can stop a specific model from using a set of MCP servers alongside a skill that touches sensitive internal data.
  • Flag or block, your call: decide whether a violation is surfaced for review or stopped outright, and set the severity that fits your risk tolerance.
  • 100+ built-in guardrails: start with more than 100 out-of-the-box security policies, with more on the way.

The result is AI governance that runs at the speed of the agents themselves, not on the cadence of a periodic scan.

From the endpoint to production

A misbehaving agent is a problem wherever it runs. Think of it like a fire alarm: the room matters (an agent near your crown jewels or in production is more urgent than one on a test box), but you want the alarm in every room.

That’s why Agent Activity is available across both OX.VibeSec and OX.Cloud, giving teams one view of agent behavior from developer endpoints through to production workloads.

We’ve also added a new LiteLLM connector. LLM proxies have become a baseline part of how organizations run AI, and this integration brings that traffic into the same picture.

Why this matters

AI security isn’t only about discovering agents or scanning the code behind them. It’s about understanding and controlling what they do while they’re running.

Agent Activity is a significant step toward unified AI visibility, detection, and runtime governance across the entire agent lifecycle, so security teams can say yes to AI adoption with confidence instead of guesswork.

Availability

Agent Activity is available today in early access for OX customers, and the experience will continue to evolve on the way to general availability.

The post Introducing Agent Activity: See What Your AI Agents Are Actually Doing appeared first on OX Security.

item.title: Security Tool Sprawl: How to Consolidate SAST, SCA, and CNAPP
item.dc:creator: OX Security
item.description:
What Is Security Tool Sprawl? Security tool sprawl is the accumulation of security tools bought to fill one gap at a time, each with its own console, policy set, and finding format, until their coverage overlaps in some places and leaves gaps in others. The result is more findings, more consoles, and less certainty about […]

The post Security Tool Sprawl: How to Consolidate SAST, SCA, and CNAPP appeared first on OX Security.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

  • Security tool sprawl is the build-up of overlapping security tools that report the same risks separately and leave gaps between them.
  • Consolidating static application security testing (SAST), software composition analysis (SCA), and cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPPs) means mapping what each tool covers, unifying findings in one shared context from code to runtime, and retiring a tool only once its coverage is proven elsewhere.
  • Sprawl costs application security (AppSec) programs in three ways: duplicate alerts for the same issue, coverage gaps at the seams between tools, and context lost between code and cloud.
  • SAST, SCA, and CNAPP overlap where the pipeline meets the cloud, through infrastructure-as-code (IaC) and container image scanning, and stay distinct at the layer each one reads.
  • The number of AppSec tools an enterprise needs is set by coverage layers, not a headcount: one source of findings per layer, and one place where those findings correlate.
  • A phased plan of inventory, map, unify, and retire consolidates without losing coverage, provided a parallel run proves parity before any tool is switched off.
  • Consolidating to cut license spend, or onto a loosely coupled portfolio of acquired products, trades one sprawl problem for another.

What Is Security Tool Sprawl?

Security tool sprawl is the accumulation of security tools bought to fill one gap at a time, each with its own console, policy set, and finding format, until their coverage overlaps in some places and leaves gaps in others. The result is more findings, more consoles, and less certainty about what is actually covered.

In application security (AppSec), the pattern is familiar. Static application security testing (SAST) covers first-party code, software composition analysis (SCA) covers open-source dependencies, and a cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP) covers cloud posture and running workloads. Secrets detection, infrastructure-as-code (IaC) scanning, container scanning, and API discovery tools sit beside them, often owned by different teams. Each new category adds another tool unless an existing platform absorbs it. AI security posture management (AI-SPM) is the latest example, and it poses the same choice between one more point tool and a move to an AI-native platform.

What Does Tool Sprawl Cost an AppSec Program?

Most security leaders already suspect they have too many tools. In 2025 research by Barracuda and Vanson Bourne covering 2,000 senior security decision-makers, 65% said they have too many security tools or vendors, and 53% said their tools can’t be integrated. Those figures cover security tooling as a whole. For AppSec teams, the cost of sprawl shows up in three specific places.

#1. Alert Duplication

One vulnerable open-source package can surface three times: as an SCA finding in the repository, as a container image finding in the registry, and as a runtime finding in the CNAPP. Each arrives with its own severity score, its own owner, and its own ticket. Triage time goes to reconciling the same issue three times over, and fixes stall while teams work out whether three tickets describe one problem or three.

#2. Coverage Gaps

Tool scopes are drawn by vendors, not by risk. IaC templates can fall between a code scanner that ignores them and a CNAPP configured only for live cloud accounts. Secrets may be left to developer-side tooling that security never sees, and APIs may go uninventoried because no tool owns them. Every tool reports clean on its own scope, and nothing reports on the seams.

#3. Context Loss

Each tool sees one layer. A cloud finding without its source code can’t be routed to the developer who owns the fix, and a code finding without runtime context can’t be ranked by whether the code is deployed, exposed, or reachable. Cloud findings that lack source-code context get patched in place or parked, while code findings are prioritized on severity alone. Both teams end up working from partial evidence.

Where SAST, SCA and CNAPP Overlap, and Where They Don’t

SAST, SCA, and CNAPP overlap where the pipeline meets the cloud, and stay distinct at the layer each one reads. SAST alone reads first-party logic, SCA alone tracks dependency versions and licenses, and a CNAPP alone sees what is deployed and running.

What Each Category Covers

The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) describes SAST as source code analysis that finds security flaws in source or compiled code, and notes that it is frequently unable to find configuration issues because they are not represented in the code. OWASP defines SCA as the process of automating application security for third-party and open-source components, including their licensing. For CNAPPs, Gartner’s mandatory features include auditing cloud configuration and identity permissions, visibility into the runtime state of workloads, and, at a minimum, IaC scanning and container registry scanning. 

That last requirement is where a CNAPP reaches back into the pipeline that code security tools already cover. Dynamic and interactive application security testing (DAST and IAST) sit beside SAST as separate testing methods with their own coverage.

Vendors Are Converging From Both Sides

Category lines are blurring from both directions. CNAPP vendors now sell SAST, AppSec vendors partner with CNAPP vendors to bring runtime context into their findings, and vendors that began in open-source dependency scanning now sell SAST alongside SCA. Category labels no longer predict which tool covers what, which makes overlap harder to see from a procurement list.

One CVE, Four Detection Points

OX’s writeup of NGINX Rift (CVE-2026-42945), an NGINX vulnerability disclosed in May 2026, shows what useful overlap looks like. OX describes finding the same vulnerability at four points between the prompt and runtime:

  1. At the Prompt: OX VibeSec stops an AI coding assistant from suggesting or installing vulnerable NGINX versions before the code is written.
  2. In the Repository: OX Code finds vulnerable NGINX versions pinned in Dockerfiles, Helm charts, Terraform modules, Kubernetes manifests, and other IaC, including in container layers.
  3. In the Running Environment: OX Cloud inventories cloud workloads, fingerprints the NGINX version on each, and confirms which vulnerable instances are loaded and exposed to the internet.
  4. Through Exploitation: OX Agentic Pentester runs a specific attack sequence against the exposed instance to produce a reproducible proof of exploit.

Overlap across lifecycle stages is useful coverage when the four detections resolve to one issue with one owner. It becomes noise when four tools file four tickets.

How Many AppSec Tools Does an Enterprise Actually Need?

There is no correct number of tools. The count that matters is one source of findings for each coverage layer, and one place where those findings correlate.

NIST’s Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF), SP 800-218, is a practical way to define those layers, because it names practices rather than products:

  • PW.4, Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software When Feasible Instead of Duplicating Functionality: Includes verifying that acquired third-party and open-source components meet security requirements, the work SCA serves.
  • PW.7, Review and/or Analyze Human-Readable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements: The work SAST serves.
  • PW.8, Test Executable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements: The work dynamic testing serves.
  • RV.1, Identify and Confirm Vulnerabilities on an Ongoing Basis: Depends on findings from every layer once software is released.

The SSDF names tools only as examples, so it describes what must be covered rather than what must be bought. It also stops at development: cloud posture and runtime sit outside its scope, and that is the CNAPP’s layer (for how the framework applies in practice, see what the SSDF asks of AppSec teams). An enterprise therefore needs coverage for first-party code, dependencies, executable testing, cloud posture, and runtime, plus one place where findings from all of them correlate. Whether that takes five tools or one platform depends on whether those findings share context.

How to Reduce Application Security Tool Sprawl: A Phased Consolidation Plan

Consolidation works best as four phases run in order, with coverage verified before anything is switched off. The pressure behind it is broad: in Cisco’s 2025 Cybersecurity Readiness Index, a double-blind survey of 8,000 security and business leaders in 30 markets, more than 77% of organizations reported complex security infrastructures, dominated by more than ten point solutions, that impede their ability to respond to threats. Because tools are retired against their contract renewal dates, expect the work to span several renewal cycles rather than a single quarter.

Inventory

Start with a complete list of every security tool in use: who owns it, when its contract renews, which repositories, pipelines, and cloud accounts it covers, and who acts on its findings. Include the shadow tools bought by individual teams, since they often cover ground the central program assumes is uncovered, or duplicate what it already runs.

Map

Plot each tool against the coverage layers above and mark three things: layers covered twice, layers covered by nothing, and findings that duplicate across tools. The map sets the order of everything that follows. Gaps are closed first, and duplicated layers become the candidates for retirement.

Unify

Bring findings from the remaining tools into one platform that correlates them across code, pipeline, cloud, and runtime, so that a single issue carries its source, its deployment, and its reachability.  On the code side, application security posture management (ASPM) tools were built for this step, correlating findings across application security scanners; consolidating SAST, SCA, and CNAPP extends the same correlation to cloud posture and runtime. Run the platform in parallel with incumbent tools for at least one release cycle, and compare what each catches before relying on the platform’s view.

Retire

Decommission a tool only when the parallel run shows its coverage is matched, its custom rules and policies have been migrated, and its alerts are routed elsewhere. Sequence retirements against contract renewal dates rather than switching everything off at once.

What Can Go Wrong When Security Tools Are Consolidated?

Consolidation done badly trades one sprawl problem for another. The most common mistakes:

  • Consolidating to Cut License Spend: Treating consolidation as a cost exercise puts savings ahead of coverage. The savings are real: in Enterprise Strategy Group research published by Omdia in 2025, 55% of respondents reported positive results from consolidating security operations tools, with cost optimization among the top advantages cited. But a platform that saves money while dropping a layer of coverage has moved the cost into risk rather than removed it.
  • Retiring Tools Before Coverage Parity Is Proven: Switching off a point tool on the strength of a vendor’s feature list rather than a parallel run, and discovering the gap after an incident.
  • Buying a Loosely Coupled Portfolio: Choosing a platform assembled from acquired products that keep separate data models and separate findings under one logo. Gartner’s mandatory CNAPP features call for a single cloud-delivered platform rather than a loosely coupled portfolio of products. Correlating findings on top of separate point tools makes them easier to administer, but it does not give them a unified risk model.
  • Losing Custom Rules in Migration: Leaving behind the custom rules, suppressions, and policy exceptions tuned in the old tool, so the new platform reopens findings that were triaged long ago.
  • Dropping Developer Workflows: Losing the integrated development environment (IDE) and pull-request checks that made a point tool usable, and pushing developers back to a security console they will not open.
  • Accepting Single-Vendor Dependence Without Exit Terms: Concentrating coverage in one platform without data export, contractual exit terms, or a fallback for critical layers.

Unifying Cloud, Code and Runtime on the OX Platform

The OX AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP) is built for the unify step: one platform, one price, and one license across four pillars that share context from prompt to runtime. It also imports findings from the SAST and SCA tools a team already runs and shows them in one view alongside findings from other scanners, so the parallel run in the unify step happens in one place before any tool is retired

OX Code covers SAST, SCA, secrets and personally identifiable information (PII) detection, software bills of materials (SBOMs), IaC, Git posture, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) security, and container security. OX Cloud adds cloud security posture management (CSPM), Kubernetes and data security posture management (KSPM and DSPM), runtime vulnerabilities and runtime events, a cloud graph with attack path mapping, and AI detection and response (AIDR) for the agents, models, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers running in the cloud.

In OX Cloud, reachability does the filtering. Misconfigurations, vulnerable packages, and supply-chain exposure that nothing can reach fall away, and each alert opens into the evidence behind it: who acted, what they touched, and what else they could have reached. OX VibeSec extends the same context upstream to the prompt, and OX Agentic Pentester extends it to proof of exploitability. Because OX’s four pillars share one context lake, a finding can be traced from the prompt or commit that introduced it to the runtime environment it threatens.

Consolidating Without Losing Coverage

Security tool sprawl costs AppSec programs duplicate alerts, uncovered seams, and context lost between code and cloud. SAST, SCA, and CNAPP overlap where the pipeline meets the cloud and stay distinct at the layer each one reads, so the goal is not fewer layers of coverage but fewer places where findings sit unconnected.

Consolidation succeeds when coverage is mapped first, findings are unified on one platform with shared context, and each tool is retired only after a parallel run shows nothing has been lost. Find out how OX could unify your cloud, code, and runtime.

FAQs

Counts vary widely with how each survey defines a tool or a vendor, so a single average is unreliable. The clearer signal is complexity: in Cisco’s 2025 Cybersecurity Readiness Index, a survey of 8,000 security and business leaders, more than 77% of organizations reported complex security infrastructures, dominated by more than ten point solutions, that impede their ability to respond to threats. For AppSec, the more useful measure is coverage per layer: whether first-party code, dependencies, cloud posture, and runtime each have one source of findings, and whether those findings correlate.

One platform can cover the capabilities of SAST, SCA, and a CNAPP, provided it correlates their findings in a shared context rather than bundling separate products under one console. Whether it can replace a specific incumbent tool is a question for evidence: run the platform alongside existing tools for at least one release cycle, and compare what each catches before retiring anything.

The main risks are coverage gaps from retiring a tool before parity is proven, lost custom rules and policy exceptions, broken developer workflows when IDE and pull-request checks change, and dependence on a single vendor without exit terms. Consolidating mainly to cut license spend adds another; savings bought by dropping coverage come back as risk. A phased plan with a parallel run before each retirement addresses most of these.

item.content:encoded:
5 days after emergency fixes shipped, 93.6% of measurable PHP instances are still exposed

On October 21, the PHP project shipped emergency releases for PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that give an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution inside the PHP engine itself. Security agencies issued urgent advisories, and some organizations pulled systems offline while they worked out their exposure.

In our first report, we found that 99.3% of the PHP instances we could measure were still unpatched after 24 hours. We kept watching. As of October 26, five days after disclosure, the picture has barely shifted – 93.6% still exposed. That’s roughly 15 out of every 16 hosts we can measure.

Approximately 1.33 million affected hosts run end-of-life PHP branches that no longer receive official fixes. For these systems, remediation may require a version update as well.

What we Measured

OX Security ran repeated Shodan queries from the first evening after disclosure through October 26, 2026. We classified each host by the PHP version it advertises publicly.

Hosts that hide their PHP version cannot be classified and are left out of every affected-versus-patched figure in this post.

Day by day: how far did patching get?

Our first scan, on the evening of October 21, found 2,224,364 PHP instances on Shodan. Of the 1,991,515 we could place in the affected range, only 245 were already on a fixed release. Five days later, that number is 127,430. That’s progress –  a slow one. 

No segment we measured has patched even a quarter of its affected hosts.

Conclusion: we missed the opportunity to get patches out the door

Remediation is too slow, while everyone panics about PHP CVEs, remediation isn’t in panic state, it barely crawls, with more headlines than fixed instances in the wild.

PHP2Shell is one of the most covered vulnerabilities of the year, and five days after the fix shipped, 93.6% of measurable instances are still exposed.

While everyone were looking at the “Steal My Bitcoin” challenge – giving a reward in the form of Crypto for whoever successfully exploits their PHP vulnerable site, we missed the opportunity to actually get our patches out the door – and now, when exploits are out there, proven in the wild and not just a speculation – we’ve left our most precious assets exposed for the next hacker to take advantage of.

The post PHP2Shell, Day 5: The Panic Hasn’t Turned Into Patching appeared first on OX Security.

item.dc:creator: Moshe Siman Tov Bustan

The rate at which critical vulnerabilities are discovered continues to outpace our ability to remediate them at scale Overview On October 21, PHP released emergency fixes for PHP2Shell, two critical […]

The post PHP2Shell: 24 hours in, 99.3% of Measurable PHP Instances Are Still Unpatched appeared first on OX Security.
item.content:encoded:
OX Security tracked over 2.2 million publicly exposed PHP instances following disclosure. Within 24 hours, only 14,151 affected systems visible on Shodan had been patched. The rate at which critical vulnerabilities are discovered continues to outpace our ability to remediate them at scale

Overview

On October 21, PHP released emergency fixes for PHP2Shell, two critical vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — that allow unauthenticated remote code execution in the PHP engine itself.

Governments and security agencies around the world urged organizations to patch immediately. Some took systems offline. But 24 hours later, our data shows just how slowly that remediation is actually happening.

OX Security tracked more than 2.2 million publicly visible PHP instances through Shodan over the 24 hours following disclosure. Of the 1,974,890 measurable instances running versions in the affected range after 24 hours, just 14,151 were showing one of the newly patched PHP versions.

That’s 0.7% patched.

Put another way, 99.3% were still not showing a patched PHP version 24 hours after emergency fixes became available.

And while patching accelerated over the course of the day, it barely dented the affected population. At our initial measurement, only 245 instances were showing a patched version. Twelve hours later, that number had risen to 4,519. After 24 hours, it reached 14,151.

We also broke the data down across popular PHP-based technologies including WordPress, phpMyAdmin, Drupal and Laravel. The pattern was consistent: Roughly 99% of the affected hosts we could measure were still not showing a patched PHP version.

The findings illustrate the challenge facing defenders as critical vulnerabilities and attacks happen faster than many organizations can remediate them. Even after an emergency patch, worldwide warnings and extraordinary attention, the overwhelming majority of the affected systems we could measure remained unpatched 24 hours later.

Methodology and limitations: OX Security queried Shodan over the 24 hours following disclosure. PHP versions were identified from version information exposed publicly by indexed hosts, including headers such as X-Powered-By. Hosts that do not expose their PHP version cannot be classified using this methodology and are not included in our affected-versus-patched calculations. Because Shodan is a continuously changing index, changes in the total number of indexed hosts should not on their own be interpreted as evidence that systems were patched, isolated or taken offline.

For a flaw of this severity, standard emergency playbooks dictate a ‘drop-everything’ response where patching and validation should take no more than an hour. Yet 24 hours later, 99.3% of affected systems remain unpatched. This gap highlights a dangerous disconnect: while deployment itself takes minutes, operational fear of breaking live production systems, complex dependencies, and delayed approvals still outweigh immediate security threats in the real world.

How Many PHP Instances Were Secured?

At our initial assessment, Shodan showed 2,224,364 publicly visible PHP instances. Of the instances whose versions we could classify, 1,991,515 were running versions in the affected range, while just 245 were showing one of the newly patched releases.

Around 233K instances contained an earlier version not vulnerable to PHP2Shell (PHP 5.3 and older). 

Twelve hours later, we identified 4,519 patched instances.

After 24 hours, that number had risen to 14,151 — just 0.72% of the measurable affected population.

What About PHP-Based Websites?

The same pattern appears across widely used PHP-based technologies, including WordPress, phpMyAdmin, Drupal, Laravel, Joomla, cPanel and Magento.

Among the affected hosts whose PHP versions we could identify through Shodan, roughly 99% were still not showing a patched PHP version after 24 hours.

The data covers only publicly indexed hosts that expose enough PHP version information for us to classify them, so it should not be read as an estimate of the total vulnerable population for any individual technology.

Conclusions

PHP2Shell triggered emergency patches, government warnings, and worldwide attention. Yet 24 hours later, 99.3% of the affected PHP instances we could measure were still not showing a patched version.

That gap matters beyond PHP.

Security teams are already dealing with a constant stream of critical vulnerabilities, active exploitation and software supply chain attacks. PHP2Shell arrived as organizations were also responding to incidents such as the LiteLLM compromise. When multiple emergency-grade issues arrive at once, the challenge is no longer simply knowing that something is critical. It is knowing what is exposed, what can actually be exploited, what matters most and what needs to be fixed first.

AI makes that problem harder. It is accelerating vulnerability research and making it easier to find and develop exploits for flaws buried in mature software. But organizations still have to identify affected systems, determine exposure, test updates, prioritize remediation and deploy fixes across real production environments.

We are getting faster at finding critical vulnerabilities than we are at removing them from the internet.

PHP2Shell may be an early indication of what that imbalance looks like at scale. If AI continues to accelerate vulnerability discovery, defenders will need to get better not only at patching quickly, but at understanding their attack surface, reducing unnecessary internet exposure and functionality, monitoring for exploitation, and prioritizing the vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual risk.

Finding vulnerabilities faster is only an advantage if defenders can fix them fast enough to keep up.

The post PHP2Shell: 24 hours in, 99.3% of Measurable PHP Instances Are Still Unpatched appeared first on OX Security.

A Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data — including Brotli-encoded HTTP responses it fetches — can be driven to write past the end of its buffer, leaking memory or executing code with […]

The post Node.js Brotli Decoder Out-of-Bounds Write (RCE) – CVE-2026-111497 appeared first on OX Security.
item.content:encoded:
On October 21, 2026, Node.js shipped security releases across all supported lines fixing a high-severity out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder. A Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data — including Brotli-encoded HTTP responses it fetches — can be driven to write past the end of its buffer, leaking memory or executing code with the process’s privileges.

What is Node.js?

Node.js is a widely used server-side JavaScript runtime that powers a large share of web backends, APIs, build tooling and serverless functions. It bundles Google’s Brotli library (`deps/brotli`) to back its built-in `zlib` Brotli support — `zlib.brotliDecompress()` / `brotliDecompressSync()`, streaming Brotli, and the transparent decoding of Brotli-encoded HTTP bodies (`Content-Encoding: br`). 

Because decompressing untrusted Brotli is common (fetched HTTP responses, uploaded or proxied payloads), a decoder memory-safety bug is reachable from ordinary traffic across a huge range of services, and a WAF does not mitigate it.

Affected versions

CVE-2026-111497 – Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write -> RCE

Brotli can split literals, commands and distances into block types and switch between them mid-stream. `DecodeBlockTypeAndLength` returned a `BROTLI_BOOL`, overloading `BROTLI_FALSE` to mean both “invalid stream” (only one block type, so a block switch is illegal) and “needs more input.” 

The block-switch callers treated that `BROTLI_FALSE` as recoverable – and `DecodeLiteralBlockSwitch` discarded the result entirely – so a malformed block switch did not stop decoding: the decoder continued with invalid state and wrote out of bounds.

Recommendations

  • Upgrade now. Node.js 22.23.4 / 24.22.1 / 26.12.1. End-of-life lines (25.x, 23.x, <= 20.x) get no fix – move to a supported line.
  • Treat Brotli decompression of untrusted input as the sensitive path. Anything that calls `zlib.brotliDecompress(Sync)` on attacker data, or fetches Brotli-encoded responses (sends `Accept-Encoding: br`), including indirectly through libraries.
  • Be wary of PoCs and “patch” scripts. Do not clone or run unverified exploit or patch scripts from public repos or social media; trust the Node.js advisory and the official releases.

The post Node.js Brotli Decoder Out-of-Bounds Write (RCE) – CVE-2026-111497 appeared first on OX Security.

All are […]

The post Three Critical Pillow CVEs: RCE and Heap Overflows in Python’s Imaging Library – CVE-2026-112900 CVE-2026-112393 CVE-2026-112403 appeared first on OX Security.
item.content:encoded:
Three CVSS 9.2 vulnerabilities in the Python imaging library, allow remote code execution and heap corruption via a single malicious image upload

Overview

Three critical Pillow vulnerabilities (CVSS 9.2, disclosed 2026-10-19) let a crafted EPS, TIFF or JPEG file trigger command execution or heap corruption in any Python service that processes user-supplied images. All are fixed in Pillow 13.0.0. The excerpts below are from the vulnerable source.

Pillow is one of the most popular Python packages, and the most popular image processing library, with an estimated 436M monthly downloads.

What is Pillow?

Pillow is an image-processing library for Python – a maintained fork of the original PIL (Python Imaging Library). It opens, converts, resizes, thumbnails and saves images across dozens of formats (JPEG, PNG, TIFF, GIF, WebP, EPS and more), and is a near-ubiquitous dependency: web frameworks (Django/Flask image handling), thumbnail and avatar pipelines, document and PDF tooling, and most Python machine-learning and computer-vision stacks pull it in directly or transitively. 

Because it routinely parses untrusted, user-supplied image bytes, a memory-safety or injection bug in Pillow is reachable from a plain file upload across a huge range of services.

Compromised Packages

CVE-2026-112900 – EPS argument injection -> RCE

Pillow renders EPS images by shelling out to Ghostscript. `EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript` passes the caller-controlled input filename after `-f` without converting it to an absolute path, so a filename that starts with `-` is parsed by Ghostscript as an option. Combined with Ghostscript’s `@argfile` syntax (a leading `@` names a file whose contents become extra arguments) and control of that file, an attacker who controls the filename Pillow opens can inject Ghostscript options and run arbitrary commands – even under the default `-dSAFER`.

CVE-2026-112393 – TIFF write heap overflow (BytesIO)

When a compressed TIFF is saved to a file-like object with no real OS file descriptor (e.g. `io.BytesIO`), Pillow routes libtiff’s output through its `_tiffWriteProc` callback. The grow loop sizes the reallocation from `state->size` (the prior buffer size) instead of `state->loc` (the current write position), so for output larger than 64 KiB libtiff can seek past the buffer and `_TIFFmemcpy` writes at `state->loc` beyond the allocation – a heap overflow, plus disclosure of stale heap bytes in the unwritten alignment gaps. Saving to a real file path (which has a `fileno()`) is not affected.

CVE-2026-112403 – JPEG draft/thumbnail heap overflow

Pillow’s JPEG decoder writes a full-width scanline into `state->buffer`, which is sized from the tile / draft extents (the unpacker), not from the JPEG header. An attacker who feeds a crafted 8-bit lossless (SOF3) JPEG to an application that requests downscaling via `draft()` or `thumbnail()` makes libjpeg produce lines wider than the buffer, overflowing the heap – crash, and potentially code execution. Newer libjpeg-turbo builds accept the malformed input that older libjpeg-turbo 2.x / IJG builds reject.

Recommendations

  • Upgrade now. `pip install -U “Pillow>=13.0.0″` and rebuild any wheels, containers or base images that vendor it. This is the only complete fix for all three CVEs.
  • Reduce the image attack surface. Accept only the formats you actually need; never pass an attacker-controlled filename to `Image.open()` for EPS, and keep the Ghostscript (`gs`) binary off hosts that process untrusted uploads (CVE-2026-112900 is only reachable when `gs` is present). Treat `draft()` / `thumbnail()` on untrusted JPEGs and TIFF saves to in-memory buffers as the sensitive paths.

The post Three Critical Pillow CVEs: RCE and Heap Overflows in Python’s Imaging Library – CVE-2026-112900 CVE-2026-112393 CVE-2026-112403 appeared first on OX Security.

item.dc:creator: Moshe Siman Tov Bustan
item.description:
LiteLLM got hijacked again: the AI gateway used to route traffic to dozens of LLM providers shipped a credential stealer with remote access built in Overview On October 21, 2026, a malicious version of LiteLLM (version 1.107.0) was published to PyPI. LiteLLM is one of the most popular open source gateways for routing requests to […]

The post LiteLLM 1.107.0 Compromised With A RAT InfoStealer appeared first on OX Security.
item.content:encoded:
LiteLLM got hijacked again: the AI gateway used to route traffic to dozens of LLM providers shipped a credential stealer with remote access built in

Overview

On October 21, 2026, a malicious version of LiteLLM (version 1.107.0) was published to PyPI. LiteLLM is one of the most popular open source gateways for routing requests to LLM providers, which means it usually sits right next to an organization’s most valuable AI and cloud credentials.

The malware combines two threats in one package: an infostealer that harvests secrets from the machine, and a remote access trojan (RAT) that lets the attacker connect remotely and control the affected machine.

The malicious code was injected only into the “wheel” package, so reviewing the repository and the “clean source” would not have revealed anything wrong. The malware also contacts the URL litellm[.]dev, which is an attacker bought domain that could easily be seen as a legitimate domain instead.

This is the second time LiteLLM has been hijacked this year. In March, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were compromised in the TeamPCP campaign. This time the attacker used different tooling and infrastructure. PyPI has since quarantined the malicious release.

Compromised Packages

Who is affected

Anyone who installed or upgraded to litellm 1.107.0 from PyPI, on any operating system (macOS, Linux or Windows)

Impact

  • The malware runs every time Python starts on an infected machine, even if the project never uses LiteLLM. Simply having the package installed is enough.
  • Once running, it can steal LLM provider API keys, cloud credentials, environment variables, and the credentials stored in a LiteLLM proxy’s own database. The stolen data is sent to a lookalike domain built to blend in with legitimate LiteLLM traffic.
  • The RAT component checks in with the attacker regularly, so a compromised machine can receive new malicious code at any time. 

Recommended Actions

Immediate Actions:

  1. Check every environment, container and CI pipeline for litellm 1.107.0, and pin LiteLLM to the safe version 1.106.0.
  2. Treat any machine that installed 1.107.0 as fully compromised. Isolate it from the network before cleaning it up.
  3. Rotate every secret that machine could reach: LLM provider API keys, cloud credentials, database passwords, SSH keys and CI tokens.
  4. If you run a LiteLLM proxy, rotate the provider keys stored in its database as well.

Technical Analysis

The malware is heavily obfuscated with multi-stage layers of command execution, the first two files that run inside the WHL file are “cook.py” and “sitecustomize.py”.

“sitecustomize.py” contains a RAT behavior and isn’t obfuscated at all, while “cook.py” contains a base64 encoded script inside.

The malware contains a configuration to check every 1 hour the configuration from the remote server. Additionally, it reads the remote C2 server from a GitHub URL, and parses the IP address of the C2 from it – then starts the connection.

The malware executes code it receives from the get_running_loop function

All of the malicious C2 RAT logic sits inside the “sitecustomize.py” file.

The infostealer logic sits under “cook.py” after deobfuscation, where it targets mostly configurations, cookies, API keys and cloud data. Crypto-stealer behavior is absent from this malware, showing that the threat actors aim to steal personal and organizational data rather than being directly financially motivated.

Reading Google Chrome profile data 

Directly accessing user passwords from the browser data

Reading command line history from both Mac, Linux and Windows, including Python history and others:

Targeting cloud platform keys such as AWS and Azure

Targeting GitHub credentials

Targeting AI tools such as Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor

The malware sends the stolen information to litellm[.]dev – which isn’t is an attacker bought domain, not a LiteLLM server.

Conclusions

Threat actors compromised LiteLLM once again, this time in a way that avoids detection by pushing the malicious code directly inside the wheel file, where many scanners and detection tools might miss it.

While this might look like “yet another PyPI malware”, hiding inside the wheel file is one of the new ways attackers use to stay hidden and bypass common detections, like in npm, whenever a new protection is added – such as blocking preinstall hooks, threat actors will go out of their ways to find new techniques to reach their goals and execute code without being detected.

If you’re yet to pin versions or add a time-based installation delay, this should be yet another wake up call to take the time and do so before it is too late. Once these passwords and credentials are out, remediation will take longer than it takes threat actors to get what they want.

How OX Can Help

Malicious dependency vetting

litellm 1.107.0 is included in the OX Security malware database.

OX customers using VibeSec who try to install the malicious version will be blocked by the platform and pointed to a safe version.

OX customers pushing code with the malicious version as a dependency will also be blocked by the OX platform pipeline scan.

  • http://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck
  • litellm[.]dev
  • https://raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain[.]txt
  • XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb
